task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-07-13, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 420,993 possessions; 90 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: organizer role (high usage, positive residual structural influence)
shaper role (low usage, positive residual structural influence)
talent control (separating role complementarity from player quality)
methodological_questions: Can lineup coverage (≥1 organizer, shaper, terminal) be separated from overall talent and role counts using within-team variation?
Does the talent control behave properly when role coverage is the predictor?
How to avoid look-ahead bias in role assignment? (roles defined from same-season data may be endogenous)
Is there enough within-team variation in coverage, given that many lineups may always satisfy ≥1 of each role?
How reliable are role classifications for low-usage players?

historical_evidence.finding: Adaptation quality (BEST-share) did not significantly predict series wins after controlling for regular-season net rating (talent). Univariate adapt beta=+0.311 p=0.1128; after talent control adapt p=0.275. n=55 series / 110 directions.

AVOID share vs winning: game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 (inflated n, team-quality confounded). Series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50, underpowered; ~80 series needed for p<0.05). Low AVOID-share bin 52.6% win, high bin 37.0%.
Season adapter profiles: top BEST-share teams (BOS, OKC) win more playoff series, while chronic AVOID teams (ORL) lose more, but confounded by team talent and small sample.
Apparent putback suppression effect on next possession disappears after matching on game state and margin; original finding was a score/context confound. TEAM ATT=-0.0038 p=0.890 after matching.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempt to isolate adaptation quality from talent in predicting series wins
failed_approaches.why: Confounding by roster quality; small sample (n=55 series) cannot separate coaching adaptation from talent.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing whether AVOID share predicts losing, independent of team quality
failed_approaches.why: Team quality confound (disciplined good teams have low AVOID share); underpowered at series level (n=50).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Linking season-level BEST-share to playoff success
failed_approaches.why: Inherent confounding with overall team talent; small sample.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Isolating a causal effect of conceding a putback on next possession performance
failed_approaches.why: Observed effect was an artifact of game-state confounding, revealed after score/margin matching.

evidence_establishes: Team-level analyses of play-type adaptation (BEST/AVOID) consistently show that talent confounding dominates, leading to untestable or inconclusive results at series level.
Game-state confounding can create spurious effects when not properly balanced (as seen in putback suppression).
Within-team or possession-level designs with adequate controls may be necessary to separate structural role effects from talent.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether within-team variation in lineup role coverage can be cleanly identified and separated from player talent.
The frequency and power of lineups lacking organizer[path] coverage within a team.
The reliability of structural-role classification at the individual player level, especially for bench players.
Any direct relationship between lineup coverage and performance.
own_inferences: With ~420k possessions and player fixed-effects or prior-season RAPM, the current dataset provides enough granularity to estimate a within-team coverage effect, avoiding the power problem of series-level studies.

Role assignment from the same season would introduce endogeneity (players' structural influence depends on team performance, which is also the outcome). A split-sample or prior-season approach can mitigate this.

The coverage binary (≥1 organizer, shaper, terminal present) may suffer from limited within-team variation: many teams could always have at least one organizer (starting point guard) and one terminal scorer on the court, so the 'without coverage' group may be sparse. This needs checking before committing to a regression design.
The definition of shaper (low usage, positive residual influence) may be noisy for players with few initiations, leading to misclassification and attenuation bias.
uncertainties: Actual within-team variation in coverage: if most lineups satisfy coverage, the effective sample size for contrast is small.
Stability of role assignments across seasons, especially for players changing teams or roles.
Potential mechanical floor: if the shaper role is rare, coverage may be almost always absent, also limiting variation.
Whether the 'organizer, shaper, terminal' framework exhaustively classifies all players—some players may be unclassifiable, affecting coverage definition.
Whether opponent defensive schemes systematically differ when facing covered vs uncovered lineups (opponent confound).

historical_effect.explanation: No prior study directly addresses lineup coverage with organizer[path] roles, so the historical evidence does not change the decision to proceed. However, the retrieved studies underscore the importance of careful talent control and warn against confounded aggregate-level designs, reinforcing the need for a within-team, possession-level approach with rigorous endogeneity safeguards.

blocking_constraints.text: The binary coverage variable may have low within-team variation; many teams might always field a lineup with all three roles, and some may never, reducing power.
Defining player roles from the same season's initiations creates a look-ahead link to the outcome, biasing estimates; roles must come from a strictly prior period.
Structural roles (especially shaper) rely on residual structural influence, which is estimated with noise for players with limited initiations; misclassification may attenuate the coverage effect.
Opponent quality and game situation may differ systematically between covered and uncovered lineups; failure to control for opponents and score state could mimic an effect.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved study directly tests lineup coverage with organizer[path] roles. Related work on adaptation quality and AVOID share at the series level could not separate role-like indicators from talent, motivating a within-team design with player-level controls.

risks.text: Coverage (≥1 organizer, shaper, terminal) may be near-constant within many teams, yielding a small effective N for the coverage contrast.
If roles are computed from the same game/season as the outcome, the coverage status is partly determined by the performance it is supposed to predict.
Shaper classification in particular is based on residual structural influence and may be noisy, diluting true complementarity effects.
Systematic differences in opponent strength, game location, and game state across covered/uncovered lineups could confound the estimated coverage effect.
If within-team variation in coverage is limited, the study may be underpowered even with 420k possessions due to high clustering and low effective degrees of freedom at the coverage level.
Subgroup analyses (by team, by half, by role) will inflate false positives unless multiplicity is controlled.

design.estimand: The causal effect of a lineup having at least one organizer, one shaper, and one terminal scorer (full coverage) on points scored per 100 possessions, relative to lineups missing at least one of these roles, net of the sum of individual player talents and opponent quality.
design.unit: Offensive possession (or 5-player stint segment), filtered to exclude garbage-time (score margin >20 in last 6 minutes).
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff possessions from NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 (420,993 possessions; 90 team-seasons), using the frozen data version of 2026-07-13.
design.power: With ~400k possessions, power to detect an effect of 2.0 points per 100 possessions (d~0.15) at alpha=0.01 is >0.80 if the within-team coverage split is at least 15% vs 85%. Exact power will be determined by simulation using the empirical within-team coverage distribution after role assignment.
controls: Player fixed effects (one-hot indicator for every player on the court) to absorb individual talent and role-specific skill.
Alternatively, pre-season RAPM (from prior 3-year blended metric) as a continuous talent control, with sensitivity checks for both specifications.
Opponent team fixed effects (or opponent average defensive rating).
Game situation controls: score margin (linear and squared), period, seconds remaining in shot clock, home/away indicator.
Lineup size (number of players) and garbage-time excluded.
falsification: Re-define roles using a random shuffle within team (keeping usage brackets but randomizing residual influence) to generate placebo coverage indicators; the placebo effect should be null.
Test whether the coverage effect disappears when only one role (e.g., only organizer) is required, showing that it is not simply a proxy for having a high-usage player.
Split by half: if coverage reflects persistent strategy rather than chance, the effect should replicate in both halves and across seasons.
Check that coverage effect is not driven by extreme outliers via winsorized outcome and leave-one-out of high-leverage teams.
design.multiplicity: Report raw per-100-possession coefficients with cluster-robust standard errors (clustered by team-season). Correct for the four main tests (overall coverage, placebo, single-role tests, half-split) using the Bonferroni-Holm procedure. All exploratory subgroup analyses (by role type, by quarter) will be clearly labeled as secondary.
design.decision_rule: Overall coverage effect is declared supported if its coefficient is positive with p<0.01 (two-sided, after multiplicity correction) and the placebo test does not reject the null at p>0.20. The design must be pre-registered with the exact role-definition period and control specification before any data inspection.
design.data_version: 2026-07-13 frozen dataset: NBA stats API per-game files 2022-23 to 2025-26, with derived play-type possession records as of that date.
